conceptBreakdown.heading: 1.1 Structural Organization & Body Symmetry
conceptBreakdown.title: 1.1 Structural Organization & Body Symmetry
conceptBreakdown.content:
### 1. Levels of Body Organization
• **Cellular Level**: Loose cell aggregates exhibiting minimal functional division of labor; true tissues and nerve nets are absent (e.g., *Porifera*).
• **Tissue Level**: Cells performing similar functions are arranged into coordinated structural tissues (e.g., *Cnidaria*, *Ctenophora*).
• **Organ Level**: Tissues assemble into functional organs dedicated to specialized physiological tasks (e.g., *Platyhelminthes*).
• **Organ-System Level**: Specialized organs integrate into complex physiological systems (digestive, circulatory, nervous, excretory) (e.g., *Aschelminthes* through *Chordata*).

### 2. Patterns of Body Symmetry
• **Asymmetry**: No single plane passing through the central axis divides the body into equal halves (e.g., most sponges, adult gastropod molluscs with shell torsion).
• **Radial Symmetry**: Any longitudinal plane passing through the central axis divides the organism into identical halves (e.g., *Cnidaria*, *Ctenophora*, adult *Echinodermata*).
• **Biradial Symmetry**: Body can be divided into identical halves by only **two vertical planes** (e.g., *Ctenophora* due to paired tentacles and ciliated comb rows).
• **Bilateral Symmetry**: Body can be divided into identical left and right halves along only **one single median sagittal plane** (e.g., *Platyhelminthes* through *Chordata*).
  - **Cephalization**: Bilateral symmetry is evolutionary linked with cephalization—the concentration of sensory receptors, interneurons, and mouth parts at the leading anterior end.
